turns.prompt_text: do odb2 devices exist for things like excavators or backhoes
turns.response_html:
Yes, but they typically use different standards and connectors than the OBD2 port found in passenger cars.

While cars use the 16-pin OBD2 (SAE J1962) standard, heavy machinery like excavators and backhoes usually utilizes the SAE J1939 protocol. Instead of the rectangular car port, you will likely find a round 9-pin Deutsch connector (often green or black).

Key Differences

  • Protocol: Heavy equipment uses J1939, which handles higher data loads for complex hydraulic and engine systems.
  • Connectors: Most construction equipment uses a circular 9-pin port, though brands like Caterpillar often use a proprietary 14-pin connector.
  • Data Depth: These devices provide "Suspect Parameter Numbers" (SPN) instead of standard automotive "P-codes."

Can you use an OBD2 device?

You cannot plug a standard car scanner directly into an excavator. However, you can use:

  1. Adapters: Cables that convert the 9-pin J1939 or 14-pin CAT port to a 16-pin OBD2 shape.
  2. Heavy-Duty Scanners: Tools like the Ancel HD series or NL102 are designed to read J1939 protocols out of the box.
  3. Manufacturer Software: Many modern machines (like John Deere or Komatsu) require proprietary laptop-based software for deep diagnostics.

For Komatsu equipment, the setup is distinct from the standard OBD2 system you’d find in a truck or car. While they use the same underlying communication "language" (CAN bus), the physical access and specific data protocols are specialized.

1. The Connector: 12-Pin Rectangular

Unlike the 16-pin OBD2 or the round 9-pin Deutsch used by many other brands, most modern Komatsu excavators and backhoes use a 12-pin rectangular diagnostic connector.

  • Location: Typically found inside the cab (under the seat or behind a side panel) or inside the main electrical compartment.
  • Adapters: If you have a high-end heavy-duty scanner, you often need a "Komatsu 12-pin to OBD2" or "12-pin to 9-pin" adapter cable to physically plug in.

2. KOMTRAX: The "Wireless OBD"

Komatsu is famous for KOMTRAX, their built-in telematics system. Instead of plugging in a device, the machine sends data via satellite or cellular signals to a web portal.

  • Data Provided: Fuel consumption, location, caution lamps, and working hours.
  • Cost: On most newer machines, this service is free for the life of the machine, meaning you can often diagnose issues from a laptop or phone without ever touching a physical port.

3. Reading Codes Without a Device

Many Komatsu excavators (like the Dash-8 or Dash-10 series) allow you to view fault codes directly on the dashboard monitor using "Service Mode."

  • The Secret Key: On many models, holding down the "4" button while pressing buttons 1, 2, and 3 in sequence will open the service menu.
  • Code Types:
    • CA Codes: Engine-related (e.g., CA689 for an engine speed sensor).
    • E Codes: General system or hydraulic errors (e.g., E02 for PC-EPC system).
    • D Codes: Electrical or circuit faults.

4. Professional Diagnostic Tools

If you need to do more than just read codes (like performing a DPF regeneration or cylinder cutout tests), you generally have two paths:

  • Official: A laptop with Komatsu Service Tool software and a communication adapter (like the Komatsu Wireless Adapter).
  • Aftermarket: Professional heavy-duty scanners like Jaltest or Texa offer "dealer-level" access to Komatsu systems, including hydraulics and engine controllers.

turns.prompt_text: is Komatsu protocol open source or can it be read
turns.response_html:
The Komatsu protocol is proprietary rather than open source, but it is not completely "closed." Because Komatsu equipment must interact with various components (like Cummins engines) and follow international regulations for fleet management, the data is a mix of standardized and secret information.

1. The Standardized Layer (J1939)

At its core, Komatsu uses the SAE J1939 protocol. This is an open industry standard for heavy-duty vehicles.

  • What you can read: Standard engine data (RPM, coolant temperature, fuel rate) is broadcast in an open format called PGNs (Parameter Group Numbers).
  • Accessibility: Any high-quality heavy-duty scanner or even a DIY Arduino/Raspberry Pi with a CAN-bus shield can "sniff" these messages because they follow a publicly documented map.

2. The Proprietary Layer (The "Secret" Data)

While the basic engine data is open, Komatsu layers its own proprietary data on top of the CAN bus.

  • What is hidden: Specialized hydraulic pressures, pump swash plate angles, and specific sensor calibrations are often sent using Proprietary PGNs.
  • The "Key": To understand these messages, you need a DBC file (a database that acts as a "dictionary" for the raw hex code). Komatsu does not release these to the public; they are baked into their official service software.
  • Encryption: Most live data isn't "encrypted" in the military sense, but it is "encoded." Without the specific map provided by the manufacturer, the data looks like random numbers (e.g., 0xFF 0x23 0x01).

3. Can it be read?

Yes, but the depth of what you can see depends on the tool you use:

Tool TypeCapabilityAccessibility
Generic J1939 ScannersBasic engine codes and live RPM/Temp.High (Easy to find)
Aftermarket Tools (Jaltest/Texa)Reverse-engineered Komatsu codes, DPF regens, and calibrations.Medium (Expensive)
Komatsu Service ToolFull "dealer-level" access, software updates, and deep hydraulics.Low (Dealers only)
DIY Sniffing (SavvyCAN)Seeing raw hex data; requires manual reverse-engineering to decode.High (Technical)

4. Open Data (ISO 15143-3 / AEMP 2.0)

If you are interested in fleet data rather than repair diagnostics, Komatsu supports the ISO 15143-3 standard. This is an "open" API that allows different brands of machines (CAT, Komatsu, John Deere) to share their location and fuel usage with a single third-party software. This is how mixed-fleet owners track all their machines in one place.

If you're trying to build a custom monitoring solution, this video demonstrates professional diagnostics on a Komatsu PC-Series excavator, showing the depth of data available when using a tool that has successfully reverse-engineered the proprietary codes.

turns.prompt_text: could you hook up a Raspberry Pi to a Komatsu machine in order to transmit information to a phone laptop or a server
turns.response_html:
Yes, you absolutely can. This is a common project for "precision construction" and remote fleet monitoring. Because Komatsu machines use the J1939 (CAN bus) protocol, a Raspberry Pi acts as an excellent bridge between the machine's heavy-duty hardware and the digital world.

Here is the blueprint for how you would set this up:

1. The Necessary Hardware

The Raspberry Pi itself cannot talk to a Komatsu machine directly because its pins (GPIO) operate at 3.3V, while a CAN bus uses differential signals that would fry the Pi.

  • CAN-Bus HAT: You need an expansion board like the PiCAN 2 or RS485 CAN HAT. These boards include a CAN controller (MCP2515) and a transceiver to safely "read" the machine's data.
  • Isolation (Highly Recommended): Construction equipment is "electrically noisy." Using an Isolated CAN HAT protects your Pi from voltage spikes when the machine starts or when heavy hydraulic solenoids fire.
  • The Physical Adapter: You will need to wire a cable from the PiCAN board (usually screw terminals or a DB9 port) to the Komatsu's 12-pin rectangular diagnostic port.

2. Software Setup (The "Translator")

Once connected, the Pi sees a stream of raw hexadecimal data. You need to turn that into something readable.

  • SocketCAN: This is a set of open-source CAN drivers built into the Linux kernel (Raspberry Pi OS). You "bring up" the interface like a WiFi connection: 
    sudo ip link set can0 up type can bitrate 250000
    (Note: Most Komatsu/J1939 systems run at 250kbps or 500kbps.)
  • can-utils: A suite of tools to sniff the data. Running candump can0 will show you a live scroll of every message the excavator is sending.

3. Transmitting to Phone, Laptop, or Server

This is where the Raspberry Pi shines compared to a standard OBD2 scanner. You can write a simple Python script to handle the data:

  • To a Phone/Laptop: You can set the Pi up as a Wireless Access Point. It can host a local web server (using Flask or Dashboard software like Grafana) so you can view live hydraulic pressures or engine RPM on your phone’s browser via the Pi's local WiFi.
  • To a Server (Cloud): If you add a 4G/LTE USB Dongle to the Pi, you can use MQTT (a lightweight messaging protocol) to send data to a remote server. This allows you to track the machine's health from miles away, essentially building your own version of Komatsu's "KOMTRAX."

4. The "Language" Barrier (Reverse Engineering)

As mentioned before, Komatsu's engine data (RPM, Temp, Fuel) follows the open J1939 standard, so the Pi can read it immediately.

However, if you want to see hydraulic pump pressure or swing motor torque, those are usually proprietary. To find them, you have to "sniff" the bus while operating the machine:

  1. Start a recording on the Pi.
  2. Move the boom.
  3. Look for the Hex ID that spiked in value exactly when the boom moved.

Comparison: DIY Pi vs. Professional Telematics

FeatureRaspberry Pi SetupKomatsu KOMTRAX
Cost~$100–$150Built-in (Subscription may apply)
CustomizationInfinite (Custom alerts, sensors)Fixed (Set by manufacturer)
Data AccessReal-time (Millisecond level)Delayed (Usually hourly/daily)
DifficultyHigh (Requires coding/wiring)Zero (Plug and play)
